name: Library and Study Pair
description: The room for work and the room for books, which are often one room asked to be two. Their requirements diverge sharply: a study wants a door that closes and a wall for a desk; a library wants continuous wall, even north light and no glare on a screen or a page.

internal_rules.statement: Continuous shelf wall of at least 10 linear ft and preferably 16. A library with three windows and a door has no wall left and becomes a sitting room with a bookcase.
North or east light on the working surface, and never a window directly facing a desk — the glare makes the best-placed desk unusable.
A real door that closes, and acoustic separation from the kitchen and any eating area. A study without a door is a desk.

Where the room is on the public side of the house it takes public trim and a formal position; where it is a working study it belongs in the family zone. Trying to be both produces a room used for neither.

attaches_to.position: one dependency — the historic use of the flanking wing
a den off the living room, usually with a wide cased opening rather than a door

expansion_logic: Split rather than enlarge: when a library has to serve as an office and a spare bedroom, the honest answer is two smaller rooms.
servicing_strategy: Data and power at the desk wall, drawn before the shelving; a library retrofitted for a workstation always loses a bay of shelf.

style_variation.note: Often in a dependency rather than the main block, which is where a modern client should be encouraged to put a home office too.
The den off the living room with a wide cased opening and built-in shelving; the built-in is definitional.
The style with the strongest claim on the room — panelled, north-lit, and the one place the idiom's darkness is an asset.
